title: How High is ‘High’? Rethinking the Roles of Dimensionality in Topological Data Analysis and Manifold Learning
claim: As ambient intrinsic dimension grows, a hidden low-dimensional manifold emerges from noisy high-dimensional data and approaches its clean latent structure.
layout: 4 panels in a row, noisy to clean, shared color bar
description: Four 3D scatter plots sit side by side. They are labelled (a) through (d) and share a vertical colorbar on the far left titled 'Latent angular position', which runs from 0 to 360 in pink, red, orange, gold, teal, blue and violet. Panel (a) is a messy, vertically smeared cloud of colored points with no clear shape. Panel (b) is a noisy U-shaped or crescent band. Panel (c) is a tighter, clearer figure-eight-like loop. Panel (d) is a clean continuous curve in the same color gradient, showing the underlying manifold. The eye goes first to the colorful point clouds and follows the progression from noise to a sharp loop. Light-blue 3D grid backgrounds frame each panel.
caption: Ambient intrinsic dimension pint, correlation rank r, and latent intrinsic dimension d at play in simulation from a toy example of the random function model with n = 1000. (a)-(c) show SVD visualisation of simulated data with respectively pint = 3, 8, 20; as pint grows, the d = 1-dimensional manifold M = {ϕ(z); z ∈Z} shown in (d) emerges in a r = 3-dimensional subspace. In this example M is homeomorphic to the latent space Z, which is a circle. See section 3 for details.
abstract: We present a generalised Hanson-Wright inequality and use it to establish new statistical insights into the geometry of data point-clouds. In the setting of a general random function model of data, we clarify the roles played by three notions of dimensionality: ambient intrinsic dimension $p_{\mathrm{int}}$, which measures total variability across orthogonal feature directions; correlation rank, which measures functional complexity across samples; and latent intrinsic dimension, which is the dimension of manifold structure hidden in data. Our analysis shows that in order for persistence diagrams to reveal latent homology and for manifold structure to emerge it is sufficient that $p_{\mathrm{int}}\gg \log n$, where $n$ is the sample size. Informed by these theoretical perspectives, we revisit the ground-breaking neuroscience discovery of toroidal structure in grid-cell activity made by Gardner et al. (Nature, 2022): our findings reveal, for the first time, evidence that this structure is in fact isometric to physical space, meaning that grid cell activity conveys a geometrically faithful representation of the real world.
